scope: Targeted primary-source review of jury roles, defence withdrawal, criminal-damage lawful excuse, section 58 reasonable excuse, and review routes in England and Wales. Not an exhaustive case digest or assessment of a live prosecution.
checks_and_qualifications: Title uses defences rather than treating all moral excuses as recognised legal defences; explains before or during trial, not only pre-trial.
Wang paragraph 14 warns against removing factual questions, not simply permission to withdraw unsupported defences. Paragraph 18 prohibits directing conviction.
2024 reference paragraphs 54–64 preserve caution and the no-reasonable-properly-directed-jury threshold, not a broad discretion to reject unconvincing explanations.
Defence withdrawal and exclusion of evidence are distinct. Section 78 PACE concerns prosecution evidence, not a general power to suppress defence explanations.
Section 5(2)(b) protects property; section 5(3) protects honest beliefs but does not dissolve the other requirements. The burden statement is expressly limited to criminal-damage lawful excuse.
Section 40(5) requires a material change for a party's variation application, alongside interests of justice and judicial initiative under subsection (4).
Section 35 preparatory-hearing appeals are not a general appeal against ordinary section 40 rulings. Conviction appeal guidance uses 28 days from conviction, not sentence.
Attorney General references do not disturb the original acquittals under section 36(7).
Webster [2026] EWCA Crim 9 is included as a later jury-independence case, not as an appeal determining all defence-withdrawal rules.
Reform proposals are labelled as our analysis, not existing procedural entitlements.
access: Wang read on Parliament's HTML pages; G and J paragraphs 79–83 checked in Parliament's PDF text.
2022 reference read on Find Case Law; 2024 reference and Webster read via official National Archives XML because web-reader HTML was unavailable.
